source.locator: lines 50-58, first formalization of the ants-and-insects entailment

findings.finding: The closing bracket for the universal premise appears after the conclusion, so the displayed entailment does not delimit its two premises and conclusion as described by the following English argument.
findings.controlling_evidence: The immediately following prose gives three separate claims—every ant is an insect, ants exist, and insects exist—and explicitly calls the first two premises and the third the conclusion.
findings.required_translation_handling: Close the universal premise before the comma, remove the trailing extra bracket after the conclusion, and add an adjacent OLTEINT-001 note.

source.locator: lines 67-84, natural-deduction and metalogical restatements of the same entailment

findings.finding: Two later restatements omit the universal premise's closing bracket and place an extra bracket after the existential conclusion.
findings.controlling_evidence: Both passages explicitly identify the universal and existential formulas as separate premises and the final existential formula as the conclusion; correctly delimited instances of the same formulas also occur in the intervening text.
findings.required_translation_handling: Move each misplaced bracket to the end of the universal premise and add an adjacent OLTEINT-002 note.

source.locator: lines 13-25, description of a structure and the general-language case

findings.finding: The general-case sentence says constants can have more than one place, conflating individual constants with multi-place predicates.
findings.controlling_evidence: The simple structure just described interprets the constant a as one object and the predicate P as a set; the general first-order vocabulary assigns arity to predicate and function symbols, while individual constants remain nullary.
findings.required_translation_handling: Use predicates, not constants, as the category that can have more than one place and add an adjacent OLTEINT-003 note.

source.locator: lines 43-67, fixed domain followed by the variable-assignment example

findings.finding: After fixing the domain as {0,1,2}, the text says a variable assignment maps to one of 1, 2, or 3, incorrectly including 3 and omitting 0.
findings.controlling_evidence: A variable assignment must map variables to elements of the declared domain, and the continuation explicitly uses value 0 for the same assignment example.
findings.required_translation_handling: Replace the list 1,2,3 with 0,1,2 and add an adjacent OLTEINT-004 note.

findings.finding: The argument v_0 is placed outside the atomic-formula braces in the universally quantified premise, leaving P without its intended argument.
findings.controlling_evidence: The paragraph immediately generalizes the example as inferring A(t) from forall x A(x), so the opening instance must be forall v_0 P(v_0).
findings.required_translation_handling: Restore v_0 inside the P atom, retain the surrounding universal scope, and add an adjacent OLTEINT-005 note.
